title: حِكَايَةُ الْعَاشِقِ وَالْمَعْشُوقِ
titleEn: The Lover and the Beloved, continued
part: Night 128 · The Lover and the Beloved, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 607–609 (Night 128, continuing directly from nights-127), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 128 continues the story that the vizier Dandān tells within the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, the story of the lover, the beloved and the go-between, and brings ʿAzīz's own telling of it to an end. He reads to Tāj al-Mulūk the rest of his dead cousin ʿAzīza's letter: the gazelle on the cloth is the work of a princess of the Camphor Islands, and ʿAzīza warns him away from her and from every woman after her. A year of grief later he sets out with the merchants of his city; passing the Camphor Islands, he learns that the maker of the gazelles is Dunyā, daughter of King Shahramān, and he weeps for what he has lost. His tale ends in verse, and Tāj al-Mulūk is set on fire by the mention of the lady Dunyā. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّامِنَةُ وَالْعِشْرُونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāminatu wa-al-ʿishrūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the eighth and the twenty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and twenty-eighth night,

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْوَزِيرَ دَنْدَانَ قَالَ لِلْمَلِكِ ضَوْءِ الْمَكَانِ ثُمَّ إِنَّ الشَّابَّ عَزِيزًا قَالَ لِتَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ فَقَرَأْتُ مَاكَتَبَتْهُ لِى بِنْتُ عَمِّي
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-wazīra dandāna qāla li-al-maliki ḍawʾi al-makāni thumma inna al-shābba ʿazīzan qāla li-tāji al-mulūki fa-qaraʾtu mā katabathu lī bintu ʿammī
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that the vizier Dandān said to the king Ḍawʾ al-Makān: Then the young-man ʿAzīz said to Tāj al-Mulūk: And I read what the daughter of my uncle had written to me,
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the vizier Dandān told King Ḍawʾ al-Makān that the young man ʿAzīz said to Tāj al-Mulūk: So I read what my cousin had written to me.
sentences.n: The night opens, as the nights often do, by going back over where the last one stopped: ʿAzīz reading the letter his dead cousin ʿAzīza left him, which the night now gives again in fuller form. mā katabathu, “what she had written”, run together in the print; lī, “to me”, written with final ى.

sentences.t: وَأَوْصَتْنِي بِهِ وَهِيَ تَقُولُ احْتَفِظْ بِهَذَا الْغَزَالِ وَلَا تَدَعْهُ يُفَارِقُكَ فَإِنَّهُ كَانَ يُؤَانِسُنِي إِذَا غِبْتَ عَنِّي
sentences.tr: wa-awṣatnī bihi wa-hiya taqūlu iḥtafiẓ bi-hādhā al-ghazāli wa-lā tadaʿhu yufāriquka fa-innahu kāna yuʾānisunī idhā ghibta ʿannī
sentences.l: And she charged me with it, and she saying: Keep-safe this the gazelle, and do not let it leave you, for it used to keep me company when you were absent from me.
sentences.i: She had charged me with it, writing: “Keep this gazelle safe, and do not let it part from you, for it kept me company whenever you were away from me.
sentences.n: awṣatnī bihi, “she charged me with it”: awṣā bi-, to entrust someone with a thing, to lay a charge on them about it; the “it” is the gazelle. wa-hiya taqūlu, “and she saying”: the letter speaks in her voice. lā tadaʿhu, “do not let it”, the jussive of wadaʿa.

sentences.t: وَبِاللَّهِ عَلَيْكَ إِنْ قَدَرْتَ عَلَى مَنْ عَمِلَتْ هَذَا الْغَزَالَ تَتَبَاعَدُ عَنْهَا وَلَا تُخَلِّيهَا تَقْرَبُكَ وَلَا تَتَزَوَّجُ بِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-bi-allāhi ʿalayka in qadarta ʿalā man ʿamilat hādhā al-ghazāla tatabāʿadu ʿanhā wa-lā tukhallīhā taqrabuka wa-lā tatazawwaju bihā
sentences.l: And by God upon you: if you gain-power over (her) who made this the gazelle, you keep-far from her, and do not let her come-near you, and do not marry with her.
sentences.i: I beg you by God: if you ever come upon the woman who made this gazelle, keep away from her; do not let her come near you, and do not marry her.
sentences.n: wa-bi-allāhi ʿalayka, “by God upon you”, the spoken adjuration, “I beg you”. in qadarta ʿalā, “if you get the power over”, if you find a way to her. tatabāʿadu, tatazawwaju: the plain imperfect used for a request, the spoken way, where Classical would put an imperative or a jussive; so also wa-lā tukhallīhā, “do not let her”, with spoken khallā and its long ī kept. tatazawwaju bihā, “marry with her”: the verb takes bi- here, as in speech.

sentences.t: وَإِنْ لَمْ تَحْصُلْ لَكَ وَلَا قَدَرْتَ عَلَيْهَا وَلَا وَجَدْتَ لَكَ إِلَيْهَا سَبِيلًا فَلَا تَقْرَبْ بَعْدَهَا وَاحِدَةً مِنَ النِّسَاءِ
sentences.tr: wa-in lam taḥṣul laka wa-lā qadarta ʿalayhā wa-lā wajadta laka ilayhā sabīlan fa-lā taqrab baʿdahā wāḥidatan mina al-nisāʾi
sentences.l: And if she does not come-to-be yours, and you do not gain-power over her, and do not find for you to her a way, then do not approach after her one of the women.
sentences.i: And if she does not fall to you, and you cannot win her or find any way to her, then go near no other woman after her.
sentences.n: taḥṣul laka, “come to be yours, fall to your lot”. The two requests sit oddly together, keep away from her if you find her, touch no other woman if you do not; the letter leaves it so, and the tale will turn on it.

sentences.t: وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ صَاحِبَةَ هَذَا الْغَزَالِ تَعْمَلُ كُلَّ سَنَهٍ غَزَالًا وَتُرْسِلُهُ إِلَى أَقْصَى الْبِلَادِ لِأَجْلِ أَنْ يَشِيعَ خَبَرُهَا وَحُسْنُ صَنْعَتِهَا الَّتِى يَعْجِزُ عَنْهَا أَهْلُ الْأَرْضِ
sentences.tr: wa-iʿlam anna ṣāḥibata hādhā al-ghazāli taʿmalu kulla sanatin ghazālan wa-tursiluhu ilā aqṣā al-bilādi li-ajli an yashīʿa khabaruhā wa-ḥusnu ṣanʿatihā allatī yaʿjizu ʿanhā ahlu al-arḍi
sentences.l: And know that the owner of this the gazelle makes every year a gazelle and sends it to the farthest of the lands, for-the-sake that her report spread, and the beauty of her craft which the people of the earth are-powerless for.
sentences.i: And know that the woman this gazelle belongs to makes a gazelle every year and sends it to the farthest lands, so that word may spread of her and of the beauty of her handiwork, which no one on earth can equal.
sentences.n: ṣāḥibat hādhā al-ghazāl, “the owner of this gazelle”: here its maker. The print writes sana, “year”, with ه for ة, as it does now and then. yaʿjizu ʿanhā, “is unable to do it”, so: which no one can match.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا مَحْبُوبَتُكَ بِنْتُ الدَّلِيلَةِ الْمُحْتَالَةِ فَوَصَلَ إِلَيْهَا هَذَا الْغَزَالُ فَصَارَتْ تَصْدِمُ بِهِ النَّاسَ وَتُرِيهِ لَهُمْ وَتَقُولُ إِنَّ لِى أُخْتًا تَصْنَعُ هَذَا وَهِيَ كَذَّابَةٌ فِي قَوْلِهَا هَتَكَ اللَّهُ سِتْرَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-ammā maḥbūbatuka bintu al-dalīlati al-muḥtālati fa-waṣala ilayhā hādhā al-ghazālu fa-ṣārat taṣdimu bihi al-nāsa wa-turīhi lahum wa-taqūlu inna lī ukhtan taṣnaʿu hādhā wa-hiya kadhdhābatun fī qawlihā hataka allāhu sitrahā
sentences.l: And as for your beloved, the daughter of the Dalīla the wily, this the gazelle reached her, and she began striking the people with it and showing it to them, and saying: Indeed to me (is) a sister (who) makes this; and she (is) a great-liar in her saying, may God rend her veil.
sentences.i: As for your beloved, the daughter of Dalīla the Wily: this gazelle came into her hands, and she took to dazzling people with it, showing it to them and saying, ‘I have a sister who makes these’; but she lies in what she says, may God tear away her cover.
sentences.n: bint al-Dalīla al-Muḥtāla, “the daughter of Dalīla the Wily”: the Nights know a famous trickster woman by this name; here she is written with the article, al-Dalīla, and the words could also be read as a description, “the daughter of the wily go-between”. taṣdimu bihi al-nāsa, literally “strikes people with it”, apparently “astonishes them with it”; the sense is not certain. The print marks the shadda in kadhdhāba, “a great liar”. hataka allāhu sitrahā, “may God rend her veil”, expose her to shame: a curse.

sentences.t: وَهَذِهِ وَصِيَّتِي وَمَا أَوْصَيْتُكَ بِهَذِهِ الْوَصِيَّةِ إِلَّا لِأَنَّنِي أَعْلَمُ أَنَّ الدُّنْيَا قَدْ تَضِيقُ عَلَيْكَ بَعْدَ مَوْتِى وَرُبَّمَا تَتَغَرَّبُ بِسَبَبِ ذَلِكَ وَتَطُوفُ فِى الْبِلَادِ وَتَسْمَعُ بِصَاحِبَةِ هَذِهِ الصُّورَةِ فَتَتَشَوَّقُ نَفْسُكَ إِلَى مَعْرِفَتِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-hādhihi waṣiyyatī wa-mā awṣaytuka bi-hādhihi al-waṣiyyati illā li-annanī aʿlamu anna al-dunyā qad taḍīqu ʿalayka baʿda mawtī wa-rubbamā tatagharrabu bi-sababi dhālika wa-taṭūfu fī al-bilādi wa-tasmaʿu bi-ṣāḥibati hādhihi al-ṣūrati fa-tatashawwaqu nafsuka ilā maʿrifatihā
sentences.l: And this (is) my charge; and I did not charge you with this the charge except because I know that the world may grow-narrow upon you after my death, and perhaps you go-abroad by cause of that and wander in the lands, and hear of the owner of this the picture, and your soul longs to the knowing of her.
sentences.i: This is my last charge to you. I lay it on you only because I know the world may close in on you after my death; perhaps because of it you will go abroad and wander through the lands, and hear of the woman who made this picture, and your soul will long to know her.
sentences.n: waṣiyya, “charge, last wish”, the word for a dying person’s instructions; awṣaytuka bi-, “I charged you with”. qad taḍīqu, “may grow narrow”: qad with the imperfect, “it may happen that”. tatagharrabu, “you will become a stranger”, go to live in foreign lands. The print writes mawtī and fī with final ى.

sentences.t: فَتَذْكُرُنِي فَمَا يَنْفَعُكَ فَلَا تَعْرِفُ قَدْرِي إِلَّا بَعْدَ مَوْتِي
sentences.tr: fa-tadhkurunī fa-mā yanfaʿuka fa-lā taʿrifu qadrī illā baʿda mawtī
sentences.l: And you remember me, and it does not profit you; and you do not know my worth except after my death.
sentences.i: Then you will remember me, and it will do you no good: you will not know my worth until I am dead.
sentences.n: fa-mā yanfaʿuka, “and it does not profit you”: the subject, the remembering, is left unstated. The print marks the shadda in illā.

sentences.t: وَاعْلَمْ أَنَّ الصَّبِيَّةَ الَّتِي صَنَعَتْ هَذَا الْغَزَالَ بِنْتُ مَلِكِ جَزَائِرِ الْكَافُورِ وَسِتُّ الْأَحْرَارِ
sentences.tr: wa-iʿlam anna al-ṣabiyyata allatī ṣanaʿat hādhā al-ghazāla bintu maliki jazāʾiri al-kāfūri wa-sittu al-aḥrāri
sentences.l: And know that the girl who made this the gazelle (is) the daughter of the king of the Islands of the Camphor, and the lady of the free-born.”
sentences.i: And know that the young woman who made this gazelle is the daughter of the king of the Camphor Islands, and the first lady among the free-born.”
sentences.n: Here ʿAzīza’s letter ends. Jazāʾir al-Kāfūr, “the Camphor Islands”, a fabled kingdom far over the sea. sitt al-aḥrār, “lady of the free-born”: spoken sitt, “lady, mistress”, in a phrase of praise; it could also be taken as a name, Sitt al-Aḥrār.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا قَرَأْتُ تِلْكَ الْوَرَقَةَ وَفَهِمْتُ مَافِيهَا بَكَيْتُ وَبَكَتْ أُمِّي لِبُكَائِي وَلَازِلْتُ أَنْظُرُ إِلَيْهَا وَأَبْكِي إِلَى أَنْ أَقْبَلَ اللَّيْلُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā qaraʾtu tilka al-waraqata wa-fahimtu mā fīhā bakaytu wa-bakat ummī li-bukāʾī wa-lā ziltu anẓuru ilayhā wa-abkī ilā an aqbala al-laylu
sentences.l: And when I read that the paper and understood what (was) in it, I wept, and my mother wept for my weeping; and I did not cease looking at it and weeping until the night came-on.
sentences.i: When I had read that paper and understood what was in it, I wept, and my mother wept to see me weep; and I went on gazing at it and weeping until night came on.
sentences.n: li-bukāʾī, “for my weeping”: li-, because of. mā fīhā, “what was in it”, and lā ziltu, “I did not cease”, are each run together in the print. ilayhā, “at it”: feminine, so most likely the paper, al-waraqa, just read; it could also be “at her”, his mother.

sentences.t: وَلَمْ أَزَلْ عَلَى تِلْكَ الْحَالَةِ مُدَّةَ سَنَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-lam azal ʿalā tilka al-ḥālati muddata sanatin
sentences.l: And I did not cease upon that the state a space of a year.
sentences.i: And I stayed in that state for a whole year.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ السَّنَةِ تَجَهَّزَ هَؤُلَاءِ التُّجَّارُ مِنْ مَدِينَتِي إِلَى السَّفَرِ وَهُمْ هَؤُلَاءِ الَّذِينَ أَنَا مَعَهُمْ فِي الْقَافِلَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda al-sanati tajahhaza hāʾulāʾi al-tujjāru min madīnatī ilā al-safari wa-hum hāʾulāʾi alladhīna anā maʿahum fī al-qāfilati
sentences.l: And after the year these the merchants from my city made-ready to the journey; and they (are) these whom I (am) with them in the caravan.
sentences.i: After the year, these merchants of my city made ready for a journey; they are the very men I am travelling with in this caravan.
sentences.n: alladhīna anā maʿahum, “whom I am with them”: Arabic repeats the pronoun inside the relative clause. The print marks the shadda in al-tujjār, “the merchants”.

sentences.t: فَأَشَارَتْ عَلَيَّ أُمِّي أَنْ أَتَجَهَّزَ مَعَهُمْ وَأُسَافِرَ لَعَلِّي أَتَسَلَّى وَيَذْهَبُ مَابِي مِنَ الْحُزْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-ashārat ʿalayya ummī an atajahhaza maʿahum wa-usāfira laʿallī atasallā wa-yadhhabu mā bī mina al-ḥuzni
sentences.l: And my mother counselled upon me that I make-ready with them and travel; perhaps I (would) be-consoled, and (would) go what (was) in me of the grief.
sentences.i: My mother urged me to make ready and travel with them, in the hope that I might find some comfort and the grief in me might leave me.
sentences.n: ashārat ʿalayya, “she advised me” (ashāra ʿalā, to counsel someone); the print marks the shadda in ʿalayya and in atajahhaza. mā bī, “what is in me”, run together in the print.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لِي اشْرَحْ صَدْرَكَ وَاتْرُكْ هَذَا الْحُزْنَ عَنْكَ وَتَغِيبُ سَنَةً أَوْ سَنَتَيْنِ أَوْ ثَلٰثَةً حَتَّى تَعُودَ الْقَافِلَةُ فَلَعَلَّ يَنْشَرِحُ صَدْرُكَ وَيَنْجَلِي خَاطِرُكَ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lī ishraḥ ṣadraka wa-itruk hādhā al-ḥuzna ʿanka wa-taghību sanatan aw sanatayni aw thalāthatan ḥattā taʿūda al-qāfilatu fa-laʿalla yansharḥu ṣadruka wa-yanjalī khāṭiruka
sentences.l: And she said to me: Open-wide your breast, and leave this the grief from you, and you are-absent a year or two years or three until the caravan returns; for perhaps your breast opens-wide and your mind clears.
sentences.i: She said to me, “Cheer your heart and put this grief away from you. Be gone a year, or two, or three, until the caravan comes home; perhaps your heart will lighten and your mind grow clear.”
sentences.n: ishraḥ ṣadraka, “open wide your breast”, take heart. wa-taghību, “and you will be away”: the plain imperfect for a request, the spoken way. fa-laʿalla yansharḥu, “perhaps … opens”: laʿalla followed straight by a verb, without the pronoun Classical wants (laʿallahu). thalātha, “three”, is printed ثلثة with a dagger alif.

sentences.t: وَلَازَالَتْ تُلَاطِفُنِي بِالْكَلَامِ حَتَّى جَهَّزْتُ مَتْجَرِي وَسَافَرْتُ مَعَهُمْ
sentences.tr: wa-lā zālat tulāṭifunī bi-al-kalāmi ḥattā jahhaztu matjarī wa-sāfartu maʿahum
sentences.l: And she did not cease coaxing me with the speech until I made-ready my merchandise and travelled with them.
sentences.i: She kept coaxing me with gentle words until I had got my goods ready and set out with them.
sentences.n: lā zālat, “she did not cease”, run together in the print. matjar, “trade goods”, what a merchant travels with.

sentences.t: وَأَنَا لَمْ تَنْشَفْ لِي دَمْعَةٌ طُولَ سَفَرِي أَبَدًا وَفِي كُلِّ مَنْزِلَةٍ نَنْزِلُ بِهَا أَفْتَحُ هَذِهِ الْخِرْقَةَ وَأَنْظُرُ فِيهَا إِلَى هَذَا الْغَزَالِ فَأَتَذَكَّرُ ابْنَةَ عَمِّي وَأَبْكِي عَلَيْهَا كَمَا تَرَانِي
sentences.tr: wa-anā lam tanshaf lī damʿatun ṭūla safarī abadan wa-fī kulli manzilatin nanzilu bihā aftaḥu hādhihi al-khirqata wa-anẓuru fīhā ilā hādhā al-ghazāli fa-atadhakkaru ibnata ʿammī wa-abkī ʿalayhā kamā tarānī
sentences.l: And I — not a tear of mine dried the length of my journey, ever; and in every halting-place we halt at, I open this the rag and look in it at this the gazelle, and I remember the daughter of my uncle and weep over her, as you see me.
sentences.i: Not once in all my journey have my tears dried. At every halt we make I open this cloth and look at the gazelle on it, and remember my cousin, and weep for her, as you see me do.
sentences.n: The print has الخرفة, a misprint for الخرقة (al-khirqa, the cloth), corrected here. wa-anā lam tanshaf lī damʿatun, “and I, not a tear of mine dried”: the sentence starts from “I” and then changes subject, as speech does; nashifa, “to dry”, used of tears and moisture. manzila, “halting-place”, a stage on the caravan road; nanzilu bihā, “we halt at”, with bi- of place.

sentences.t: فَإِنَّهَا كَانَتْ تُحِبُّنِي مَحَبَّةً زَائِدَةً وَقَدْ مَاتَتْ مَقْهُورَةً مِنِّي وَمَافَعَلْتُ مَعَهَا إِلَّا الضَّرَرَ وَهِيَ لَمْ تَفْعَلْ مَعِي إِلَّا الْخَيْرَ
sentences.tr: fa-innahā kānat tuḥibbunī maḥabbatan zāʾidatan wa-qad mātat maqhūratan minnī wa-mā faʿaltu maʿahā illā al-ḍarara wa-hiya lam tafʿal maʿī illā al-khayra
sentences.l: For she used to love me with a love exceeding; and she died crushed-with-grief from me, and I did not do with her except the harm, and she did not do with me except the good.
sentences.i: For she loved me beyond measure, and she died heartbroken because of me. I never did her anything but harm, and she never did me anything but good.
sentences.n: maqhūra, “overpowered”, crushed by a grief one cannot answer; minnī, “from me”, because of me. faʿala maʿa, “do with”, the spoken way of saying “do to”; mā faʿaltu is run together in the print, which also marks the shaddas in tuḥibbunī, maḥabba and the first illā.

sentences.t: وَمَتَى رَجَعَتِ التُّجَّارُ مِنْ سَفَرِهِمْ فَأَنَا أَرْجِعُ مَعَهُمْ وَتَكْمُلُ مُدَّةُ غِيَابِي سَنَةً كَامِلَةً وَأَنَا فِي حُزْنٍ زَائِدٍ
sentences.tr: wa-matā rajaʿati al-tujjāru min safarihim fa-anā arjiʿu maʿahum wa-takmulu muddatu ghiyābī sanatan kāmilatan wa-anā fī ḥuznin zāʾidin
sentences.l: And when the merchants return from their journey, then I return with them, and the space of my absence is-complete a full year, and I in grief exceeding.
sentences.i: When the merchants go home from their journey I shall go home with them, and my absence will have lasted a full year, all of it in deep grief.
sentences.n: rajaʿat al-tujjāru, “the merchants return”: a feminine verb before a broken plural of men, as often; after matā, “when(ever)”, the perfect points to the future.

sentences.t: وَمَاجَدَّدَ هَمِّي وَحُزْنِي إِلَّا أَنِّي جُزْتُ عَلَى جَزَائِرِ الْكَافُورِ وَقَلْعَةِ الْبَلُّورِ وَهِيَ سَبْعُ جَزَائِرَ وَالْحَاكِمُ عَلَيْهِمْ مَلِكٌ يُقَالُ لَهُ شَهْرَمَانُ وَلَهُ بِنْتٌ يُقَالُ لَهَا دُنْيَا
sentences.tr: wa-mā jaddada hammī wa-ḥuznī illā annī juztu ʿalā jazāʾiri al-kāfūri wa-qalʿati al-ballūri wa-hiya sabʿu jazāʾira wa-al-ḥākimu ʿalayhim malikun yuqālu lahu shahramānu wa-lahu bintun yuqālu lahā dunyā
sentences.l: And nothing renewed my care and my grief except that I passed by the Islands of the Camphor and the Castle of the Crystal — and they (are) seven islands, and the ruler over them (is) a king called Shahramān; and to him (is) a daughter called Dunyā.
sentences.i: And what renewed my sorrow and grief was that I passed by the Camphor Islands and the Crystal Castle. They are seven islands, and the ruler over them is a king called Shahramān, who has a daughter called Dunyā.
sentences.n: mā jaddada, “nothing renewed”, run together in the print, which marks its shadda. juztu ʿalā, “I passed by” (jāza). ʿalayhim, “over them”: a masculine plural pronoun for the islands, as if for their people. Dunyā, “the world”, a woman’s name.

sentences.t: فَقِيلَ لِي إِنَّهَا هِيَ الَّتِي تَصْنَعُ الْغِزْلَانَ وَهَذَا الْغَزَالُ الَّذِي مَعَكَ مِنْ جُمْلَةِ رَقْمِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qīla lī innahā hiya allatī taṣnaʿu al-ghizlāna wa-hādhā al-ghazālu alladhī maʿaka min jumlati raqmihā
sentences.l: And it was said to me that she, she (is) the one who makes the gazelles, and this the gazelle which (is) with you (is) from the sum of her embroidery.
sentences.i: I was told that it is she who makes the gazelles, and that this gazelle you are holding is one of her embroideries.
sentences.n: raqm, “embroidery, figured work” in a cloth. min jumlati, “from the whole of”, one among.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا عَلِمْتُ ذَلِكَ زَادَتْ بِيَ الْأَشْوَاقُ وَغَرِقْتُ فِي بَحْرِ الْفِكْرِ وَالِاحْتِرَاقِ فَبَكَيْتُ عَلَى رُوحِي لِأَنِّي بَقِيتُ مِثْلَ الْمَرْأَةِ وَلَا حِيلَةَ لِي وَمَا بَقِيَ مَعِي آلَةٌ مِثْلَ الرِّجَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ʿalimtu dhālika zādat biya al-ashwāqu wa-ghariqtu fī baḥri al-fikri wa-al-iḥtirāqi fa-bakaytu ʿalā rūḥī li-annī baqītu mithla al-marʾati wa-lā ḥīlata lī wa-mā baqiya maʿī ālatun mithla al-rijāli
sentences.l: And when I knew that, the longings increased in me, and I drowned in the sea of the thought and the burning; and I wept over my soul, because I had become like the woman, and no means (is) to me, and there did not remain with me an organ like the men.
sentences.i: When I learned that, my longings grew, and I drowned in a sea of brooding and burning. I wept for myself, for I had become like a woman, with no way out, and nothing was left on me of what men have.
sentences.n: zādat biya, “increased with me”, i.e. in me. al-ashwāq, al-iḥtirāq: the rhyme of sajʿ. ʿalā rūḥī, “over my soul”, over myself. āla, “instrument, organ”: ʿAzīz speaks of what the lady cut from him in Night 126.

sentences.t: وَإِنِّي مِنْ يَوْمِ فِرَاقِي لِجَزَائِرِ الْكَافُورِ وَأَنَا بَاكِى الْعَيْنِ حَزِينُ الْقَلْبِ وَلِي مُدَّةٌ عَلَى هَذَا الْحَالِ
sentences.tr: wa-innī min yawmi firāqī li-jazāʾiri al-kāfūri wa-anā bākī al-ʿayni ḥazīnu al-qalbi wa-lī muddatun ʿalā hādhā al-ḥāli
sentences.l: And I, from the day of my parting from the Islands of the Camphor — and I (am) weeping of eye, sad of heart; and to me (is) a while upon this the state.
sentences.i: Ever since the day I left the Camphor Islands I have gone with weeping eyes and a sorrowing heart, and I have been so for a long while now.
sentences.n: wa-innī … wa-anā: the sentence begins with “I” and begins again, as speech does. firāqī li-, “my parting from”, with li- where Classical has a direct object. bākī al-ʿayn, ḥazīn al-qalb, “weeping of eye, sad of heart”; the print writes bākī with final ى. hādhā al-ḥāl: ḥāl taken as masculine.

sentences.t: وَمَا أَدْرِي هَلْ يُمْكِنُنِي أَنْ أَرْجِعَ إِلَى بَلَدِي وَأَمُوتَ عِنْدَ وَالِدَتِى أَوْلَا وَقَدْ شَبِعْتُ مِنَ الدُّنْيَا
sentences.tr: wa-mā adrī hal yumkinunī an arjiʿa ilā baladī wa-amūta ʿinda wālidatī aw lā wa-qad shabiʿtu mina al-dunyā
sentences.l: And I do not know whether it is-possible for me that I return to my country and die beside my mother, or not; and I have had-my-fill of the world.
sentences.i: I do not know whether I shall be able to go back to my own country and die at my mother’s side, or not; I have had my fill of this world.
sentences.n: aw lā, “or not”, run together in the print as اولا. A faint mark over the wāw could be a shadda, which would give awwalan, “first” (“and die at my mother’s side first”); “or not” suits the question better, so it is read here. shabiʿtu mina al-dunyā, “I am sated with the world”, weary of living.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ بَكَى وَأَنَّ وَاشْتَكَى وَنَظَرَ إِلَى صُورَةِ الْغَزَالِ وَجَرَتْ دُمُوعُهُ عَلَى خُدُودِهِ وَسَالَتْ وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ هَذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: thumma bakā wa-anna wa-ishtakā wa-naẓara ilā ṣūrati al-ghazāli wa-jarat dumūʿuhu ʿalā khudūdihi wa-sālat wa-anshada yaqūlu hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: Then he wept and moaned and complained, and looked at the picture of the gazelle, and his tears ran on his cheeks and flowed; and he recited, saying these the two verses:
sentences.i: Then he wept and moaned and lamented, and looked at the picture of the gazelle, and his tears ran down his cheeks and streamed, and he recited these two verses:
sentences.n: anna, “he moaned” (yaʾinnu). The tale steps back out of ʿAzīz’s own telling: the vizier Dandān is speaking again. hādhayni al-baytayni, “these two verses”, the object of yaqūlu.

sentences.t:
وَقَائِلٍ قَالَ لِيْْ لَابُدَّ مِنْ فَرَجٍ * فَقُلْتُ لِلْغَيْظِ كَمْ لَابُدَّ مِنْ فَرَجٍ
فَقَالَ لِي بَعْدَ حِينٍ قُلْتُ يَا عَجَبِيْ * مَنْ يَضْمَنُ الْعُمْرَ لِي يَا بَارِدَ الْحُجَجِ
sentences.tr:
wa-qāʾilin qāla lī lā budda min farajin * fa-qultu li-al-ghayẓi kam lā budda min farajin
fa-qāla lī baʿda ḥīnin qultu yā ʿajabī * man yaḍmanu al-ʿumra lī yā bārida al-ḥujaji
sentences.l:
And (many) a sayer said to me: (There is) no escape from relief. * And I said for vexation: How many (times) ‘no escape from relief’!
And he said to me: After a time. I said: O my wonder! * Who guarantees the life-span to me, O cold of the arguments?
sentences.i:
Many a one has told me, “Relief must surely come,” * and I said in my vexation, “How often, ‘Relief must come’!”
“After a while,” he said. I said, “How strange! * Who will promise me I live so long, you with your cold reasons?”
sentences.n: wa-qāʾilin, “and (many) a sayer”: wa- with the genitive, “many a one”. li-al-ghayẓi, “for vexation”: li- of cause. bārid al-ḥujaj, “cold of arguments”, one whose reasons have no life in them. The verse is copied as the print points it.

sentences.t: وَقَوْلُ الْآخَرِ
sentences.tr: wa-qawlu al-ākhari
sentences.l: And the saying of the other:
sentences.i: And the words of another poet:

sentences.t:
اَللّٰهُ يَعْلَمُ اَنِّيْ بَعْدَ فُرْقَتِكُمْ * بَكَيْتُ حَتَّى اسْتَلَفْتُ الدَّمْعَ بِالدَّيْنِ
فَقَالَ لِيْ عَاذِلِيْْ اِصْبِرْ تَنَالُهُمْ * فَقُلْتُ يَا عَاذِلِي اَلصَّبْرُ مِنْ اَيْنِ
sentences.tr:
allāhu yaʿlamu annī baʿda furqatikum * bakaytu ḥattā istalaftu al-damʿa bi-al-dayni
fa-qāla lī ʿādhilī iṣbir tanāluhum * fa-qultu yā ʿādhilī al-ṣabru min ayni
sentences.l:
God knows that I, after your parting, * wept until I borrowed the tear on the debt.
And my blamer said to me: Be-patient, you will-attain them. * And I said: O my blamer, the patience — from where?
sentences.i:
God knows that since you went away from me * I have wept until I borrowed tears on credit.
My critic told me, “Be patient, and you will win them.” * I said, “My critic, and where is patience to come from?”
sentences.n: istalaftu al-damʿa bi-al-dayni, “I borrowed tears on debt”: his own are spent. ʿādhil, “the blamer”, the stock figure of love poetry who reproaches the lover. tanāluhum, “you will reach them”: the print points the indicative where Classical grammar wants the jussive (tanalhum) after an imperative. min ayni, “from where?”: ayna takes a kasra for the rhyme with al-dayni. The verse is copied as the print points it.

sentences.t: وَهَذِهِ حِكَايَتِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ فَهَلْ سَمِعْتَ أَغْرَبَ مِنْ هَذَا الْحَدِيثِ
sentences.tr: wa-hādhihi ḥikāyatī ayyuhā al-maliku fa-hal samiʿta aghraba min hādhā al-ḥadīthi
sentences.l: And this (is) my tale, O the king; so have you heard (anything) stranger than this the story?
sentences.i: “And that is my story, O king. Have you ever heard a stranger tale than this?”
sentences.n: ʿAzīz speaks once more, closing his tale; he calls Tāj al-Mulūk, a king’s son, “king”.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ غَايَةَ الْعَجَبِ وَإِنَّهُ لَمَّا سَمِعَ قِصَّةَ الشَّابِّ انْطَلَقَتْ فِي فُؤَادِهِ النِّيرَانُ بِسَبَبِ ذِكْرِ السِّتِّ دُنْيَا وَجَمَالِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjaba tāju al-mulūki ghāyata al-ʿajabi wa-innahu lammā samiʿa qiṣṣata al-shābbi inṭalaqat fī fuʾādihi al-nīrānu bi-sababi dhikri al-sitti dunyā wa-jamālihā
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk wondered the utmost of wonder; and he, when he heard the story of the young-man, the fires were-let-loose in his heart by cause of the mention of the lady Dunyā and her beauty.
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk was utterly amazed; and when he had heard the young man’s story, fire broke out in his heart at the mention of the lady Dunyā and her beauty.
sentences.n: wa-innahu lammā, “and he, when …”: the storyteller’s inna, opening a new turn of the tale. al-sitt, “the lady”, the spoken title before a woman’s name.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
